news.title: U.S. Department of Education Announces Additional Ed-Flex Approvals to Reach Historic 25-State Milestone
news.content:
August 21, 2026
Arizona, Nevada, and South Carolina Approved for Ed-Flex Authority to Reduce Federal Burden
Today, the U.S. Department of Education announced the approval of Arizona, Nevada, and South Carolina’s Ed-Flex applications, marking a historic milestone as 25 states now have access to this flexibility. With half the nation participating, Ed-Flex is reshaping how education agencies respond to local needs and drive student academic achievement.
Ed-Flex allows states to waive certain federal requirements that could hinder local efforts to improve education. Under this authority, state educational agencies (SEAs) can waive select statutory or regulatory requirements for districts and schools without first having to submit those waivers to the U.S. Department of Education for review and approval. For example, Ed-Flex states can allow districts flexibility on how to spend their Student Support and Academic Enrichment funds, releasing them from rigid spending caps.
Today’s approval is another step in the Trump Administration’s mission to return education to the states. Half of states now have greater decision-making authority and autonomy over their districts and schools, empowering them to better respond to the needs of students and families.
“Reaching 25 Ed-Flex states is a watershed moment that proves the paradigm is shifting in American education,”
said Kirsten Baesler, Assistant Secretary for the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education.
“Innovation does not flow from top-down mandates, but rather it thrives when state and local leaders are given the regulatory freedom to adapt and respond directly to their students. This milestone is a call for every state leader to build on the momentum and prioritize placing decision-making where it belongs – closest to the student.”
“This is a welcome decision that allows Arizona’s local district and charter schools to have more control over how they spend money for education,”
said Tom Horne, Arizona Superintendent of Public Instruction.
“People at the local level have far more knowledge to make good decisions as opposed to out-of-state decision makers. Having Ed-Flex authority will result in better decisions and better use of federal funds to improve student achievement.”
“The U.S. Department of Education’s approval of Ed-Flex for Nevada is an important step toward providing more flexibility for our districts and schools in the use of federal Title funding,”
said Dr. Victor Wakefield, Nevada Superintendent of Public Instruction.
“Nevada’s participation in Ed-Flex is the direct result of valuable feedback provided earlier this year during my statewide listening tour and complements broader efforts led by Governor Joe Lombardo and the Nevada Legislature to modernize and streamline processes. Our shared goal is to focus time and resources on what matters most: high-quality teaching and learning.”
“The best education policies don't create more hoops to jump through. They create more opportunities for students to learn, grow, and succeed. That's exactly what this flexibility allows us to do,”
said Ellen Weaver, South Carolina Superintendent of Education.
“We are grateful to the U.S. Department of Education for approving South Carolina's Ed-Flex application and for its confidence in our state's ability to responsibly leverage this flexibility to better support districts, empower educators, and keep the focus where it always belongs: on students and their success.”
Background:
On March 20, 2025, President Trump signed
Executive Order 14242
,
Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities.
Since then, ED has taken steps to break up the federal education bureaucracy, expand education freedom, and empower states by sharing guidance and resources on existing flexibilities in statute to spend federal education dollars.
ED
sent a letter
encouraging states to consider applying for Ed-Flex on September 17, 2025. To date, 25 states have Ed-Flex Authority. View the full list of participating states
here
.

news.title: U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon Visits Virginia on Returning Education to the States Tour
news.content:
August 20, 2026
Winchester, VA –
Today, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, alongside Congressman Ben Cline, visited the Emil & Grace Shihadeh Innovation Center in support of the
Returning Education to the States Tour
. Secretary McMahon toured the center, which is a career and technical education program apart of Winchester Public Schools, to learn more about how they are Making America Skilled Again.
During the visit, Secretary McMahon and Congressman Cline greeted students as they arrived for the new school year before touring the center for a firsthand look at the Professional Skills Academy and Health Science Academy.
“Career and technical education gives students the skills, experience, and confidence they need to succeed in the workforce,”
said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“As we return education to the states, the Trump Administration is highlighting and learning from innovative programs that are preparing students for the careers of tomorrow. The Emil & Grace Shihadeh Innovation Center is a great example of what is possible when educators and communities prioritize hands-on learning and connect students directly with real-world opportunities.”
“Career and Technical Education programs equip students with the skills, training, and hands-on experience they need to succeed in the workforce, which is why I have supported increased funding for them in the House. We must continue strengthening these pathways, so every student has the opportunity to gain the tools they need to build a successful future,”
said Congressman Ben Cline.
“Thank you, Secretary McMahon, for coming to Virginia's 6th District to speak with one of our fantastic trade schools, the Emil & Grace Shihadeh Innovation Center, and for promoting policies that help our students and build our workforce.”
Background
On her Returning Education to the States Tour, Secretary McMahon is traveling to all 50 states to hear directly from teachers, parents, students, and community leaders about what is working in their communities and compile a toolkit of best practices to share with states across the nation.  Learn more about Secretary McMahon’s Returning Education to the States Tour
here.

news.title: U.S. Department of Education Releases Guidance on Responsible Use of Education Technology in the Classroom
news.content:
August 20, 2026
Today, the U.S. Department of Education (the Department) released new guidance to help states, school districts, educators, families, and education technology providers make informed decisions about the responsible use of technology in classrooms.
As technology increasingly plays a key role in education, states and local communities should continue to lead decisions about how such tools are used. Today’s guidance, a “Dear Colleague Letter (DCL),” encourages a focus on instructional value over recreational engagement when selecting and using technological tools in the classroom. It also urges states to pair innovation with evidence, educator judgement, transparency for parents, and a relentless focus on student outcomes.
As states chart their path forward, the Trump Administration calls upon them to preserve the human-centered core of teaching while seizing the powerful opportunities our modern world offers to nurture every student’s academic potential.
“Cell phones and algorithm-driven social media distract students from learning and undermine the focused classroom environments they need to succeed. States and schools are right to take steps to remove those distractions,”
said Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler.
“In contrast, instructional technologies should be judged by their impact on learning, not simply whether they happen on a screen. The same tools that can distract during recreational use can also expand access to advanced courses, support students with disabilities, and help close learning gaps, when used wisely. The Trump Administration hopes that as states ground their decisions in evidence and educational value, technology is a meaningful tool to improve student outcomes.”
Background:
The DCL maintains that technology use should have a clear instructional purpose, be backed by independent evidence, be transparent in design and data use, and be supported by strong implementation:
States and districts should focus on learning impact, choose tools with proven results, review effectiveness regularly, and support educator training.
Providers should build evidence-based tools that strengthen instruction, minimize unnecessary screen time, and offer practical implementation support.
Schools and providers should build opportunities for greater transparency around how and when technology is used, including how much time students spend on screens, how tools are being implemented, and whether that use is contributing to meaningful learning outcomes.
When evidence shows a tool is not improving learning, schools must be willing to change course, and when repeated findings confirm persistent shortcomings, they should remove it altogether.
Every education technology product should be able to satisfy five straightforward questions:
What learning problem does it solve?
When should it be used?
For whom should it be used?
For how long should it be used?
What evidence demonstrates that it improves student learning?
This letter follows a
July 2025
letter to states from U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon that outlined five principles for the responsible use of AI: education technologies should be educator-led, ethical, accessible, transparent, and protective of student data.
